topics.title: Cool Property of 782
topics.text:
Take the number $782$ and cube it. You get $478211768$. Notice anything interesting? The number $782$ appears inside its cube! So, let's try to find more numbers like this. To make this more interesting, the numbers you find must follow two rules:



- The number must end with a nonzero digit.

- Your solution does not count if the number appears at the end of its cube; it must appear somewhere else. (So, $24$ is not a solution even though $24^3 = 13824$.)



I gave $782$ as an example. It turns out this is the only three-digit solution that follows the above rules, but there are two solutions with two digits.



$32^3 = \underline{32}768$

$56^3 = 17\underline{56}16$



The number $32$ is a more interesting case because it is the first number in a family of numbers which appear at the beginning of their cube. See if you can figure out what "family" I am referring to, as well as why this happens.



I found several different solutions with Python which follow both of the above rules. I'm just curious if there are an infinite number of solutions which follow the two rules. What do you think?

topics.title: k Mock AMC
topics.text:
Hey guys,



So I've recently written a mock AMC-like test that I thought I'd release here for practice.  Details below:



HOW TO PARTICIPATE:

I don't want to have a big sign-up process, because then people get confused, don't see the test, don't sign up because they don't think it'll ever happen, etc.  So I've just uploaded the test in the attachment.  Feel free to PM me your answers - Add if you are in middle school or high school.  People who are in 8th this year, going into 9th next year count as middle schoolers.  Only middle schoolers are eligible for the countdown - Test-based results will include a MS division and a mixed division - All middle schoolers are considered in the MS division, and all participants are considered in the mixed division.



COUNTDOWN:

Yes, I know this is a mock AMC, but I just couldn't resist the urge to hold a countdown round.  It'll take place on FTW - Time not confirmed.  The top ten people who show up, or all if there's less than ten participate - It'll be done ladder-style.  I have a tie-breaker question in there, so there are no ties.



FORMAT:

The general format will be the same as the AMC 8:  No penalty for guessing, 25 questions, 40 minutes.  However, some of the questions are not multiple choice, mostly because there's no reason they particularly need multiple choices.  Also, don't expect it to be even close to AMC 8 level - Some of the questions will be too easy, some will be too hard.  This is my first mock test, and it's not at all super serious - Hopefully you'll still like it, but it won't be the most professional mock test ever written.



Due to my early summer schedule, I won't have time to grade the first week of June - THerefore I'm closing official participation on June 8th.  Countdown will be the next weekend, most likely.  As soon as participation closes, I'll post the answers - PM me if there are any issues, which there likely will be.  I probably forgot something in this post - Ask and I'll fix it.



Thanks for reading the post - If you want to participate, download the attached file and PM me your answers, as well as if you are in middle school or high school.  Good luck!

topics.title: k MATHCOUNTS posting guidelines
topics.text:
Advice on Posting about MATHCOUNTS



I would like to make a post about MATHCOUNTS problems from this competition year. When can I do that?



Once the problems from a 2018-2019 round are posted on the MATHCOUNTS official web page, you can discuss that round.



Do not post anything at all about School MATHCOUNTS until the School problems are posted on the official MATHCOUNTS web page. Do not post anything at all about Chapter MATHCOUNTS until the Chapter problems are posted on the official MATHCOUNTS web page. Do not post anything at all about State MATHCOUNTS until the State problems are posted on the official MATHCOUNTS web page.



Do not say anything at all about a competition until its problems are posted on the MATHCOUNTS site. Do not say whether it was difficult or easy. Do not say that you sillied on so many problems. Do not say that you got wrecked by geometry. Do not say how many points you earned. Do not say anything about how well anyone else did.



You can say your rank. And that is it.





Where can I get MATHCOUNTS problems from the past?



You can buy them from MATHCOUNTS. No one should be using the AoPS site to trade collections of old MATHCOUNTS problems. No one should be using the AoPS site to help you find links to other sites that share collections of old MATHCOUNTS problems.





Can I discuss old problems on AoPS?



Before posting an old MATHCOUNTS problem on AoPS, use the search feature to determine if there is already a thread discussing that particular problem. If there is, then check to see the content in that thread serves your purposes. You can bump an old thread if you have something new and useful to add to it. If there aren't any threads that meet your needs, you can start a new thread. (Do not report users for bumping old threads if they have something to add to the discussion about the problem. Do not report users for starting new threads about problems.)



When you do start a new thread about a MATHCOUNTS problem, please make it clear when it was from, whether it was School, Chapter, etc., whether it was Sprint, Target, etc. You can do that in the title and/or with a tag.

There aren't too many candies I can find around, so I decide I'll trick or treat there, as well! On the way, I make friends with a Hallo-gician (a Halloween magician) that can spawn infinitely many bags of three possible capacities - 11, 100, and 101. First, the two of us try separating the candy into the different bags all by themselves. I have the smallest possible amount of candy to match the following circumstances: If I use $11$-sized bags, I will have $6$ candies left over, if I use $100$-sized bags I have $95$ candies left over, and if use $101$-sized bags I have $99$ candies left over.



Instead, I try to pack the candies strategically to use the least number of bags possible. How many bags do I end up using with this new strategy? I hope it's not too many because I can't carry that much :/.  :showoff:

a) I go to a haunted house  :maybe:

b) my friend dares me to wear a funny costume  :rotfl:

topics.title: Five 5s.
topics.text:
Before we get to this, let us first discuss about Four 4s.



Four 4s is a famous recreational math puzzle, which involves trying to express every positive integer using exactly four 4s, and a specific set of operations.

For example: $69 = (4 - .4 + 4!)/.4$



In most versions of this puzzle, only the four basic operations are allowed (addition, subtraction, multiplication and division), as well as exponentiation, square roots, and factorials. Though, some versions may allow the use of decimal points, repeating decimals, arbitrary roots, and the gamma function, in order to reach higher and specific numbers.



The creator of The Definitive Four Fours Answer Key had listed answers to Four 4s of integers from 0 to 40,000.



However, I haven't seen anyone talk about Five 5s as much as Four 4s is. So I believe that I might be the first person to do so.





I aim to express the integers from 0 to 10000 using five 5s. Currently, I have found answers to more than 3000 integers using five 5s. I have made a list of them  here.



The valid operations are:

Valid operationsSome basic ones:

- Addition ($5+5$)

- Subtraction ($5-5$)

- Multiplication ($5\cdot5$)

- Division ($5/5$)

- Factorial ($5!$)

- Exponents ($5^5$)

- Decimals ($.5$)

- Implied concatenation ($55$). Note that things like $5!.5$ is not allowed.



Some slightly ugly ones:

- Repeating decimals ($.\overline5$). Note that $.\overline5=\frac59$

- Square roots ($\sqrt5$)

- Arbitrary roots ($\sqrt[5]5$)



Some really ugly ones:

- Gamma function ($\Gamma(5)$)

- Percent ($5\%$). Note that $5\%=.05$



Some avoid-it-as-much-as-you-can ones:

- Summations ($\sum$)

- Products ($\prod$)

- Limits ($\lim$)

- Integrals ($\int$)




Here are also additional rules I wanted to include:

Some additional rules I made- You are not allowed to use constants. Some examples include $\pi,e,i,\infty$.

- You cannot use the floor/ceiling/GIF function or other "rounding" functions. Such as using $[\sqrt5]$ to get 2.

- You cannot use increment functions, or anything alike that could be exploited to give every solution (this breaks the fun of the game). For example, solutions like $((55++)++)++$ are not allowed.

- In addition to the rule above, logarithms aren't allowed. This is because there is a way to exploit this function:

$$n=\frac{\ln\ln\left(\underbrace{\sqrt{\sqrt{\cdots\sqrt5}}}_{\text{n times}}\right)-\ln\ln5}{\ln(.5)}+5-5$$- Trigonometric functions also aren't allowed. You are not allowed to use $\sin,\cos,\tan,$ etc. There is also a way to exploit them:

$$n=\underbrace{\sqrt[-.5]{\sin(\tan^{-1}(\sin(\tan^{-1}(...(\sin(\tan^{-1}(\tfrac55)))...))}}_{\text{n times}}+5-5$$- Summations, Products, Limits, Integrals, etc. are allowed. But you can only use the same variable up to 5 times. (For example, you can only use at most five $n$'s in the solution)

- Another rule regarding Summations, Products, Limits and Integrals. You are not allowed to nest one inside another.

- You are allowed to use fractional values for factorials or Gamma functions. For example, you can have $(.5)!$ in order to get $\frac{\sqrt\pi}2$.






Here are some special numbers I found:

$$69=5!\cdot.5+\frac{5 - .5}{.5}$$$$420=((5+\tfrac55)!+5!)\cdot.5$$$$1337=\Gamma(5)\cdot55.5+5$$$$2018=\frac{\frac5{.5\%}+\frac5{.\overline5}}{.5}$$



Now, I face the following questions:



Is it possible to express the following numbers with five 5s and using only the basic operations?

$172,188,201,223,227,253,279,281,307,311$



Is it possible to express the following numbers with five 5s using only the basic operations and the slightly ugly ones?

$292,308,343,347,353,367,373,411,453,454$



Is it possible to express the following numbers with five 5s and without using the avoid-it-as-much-as-you-can operations?

$1087,1227,1233$



Is it possible to express the following numbers with five 5s using any of the operations stated above?

$1307,1331,1342,1343,1346,1347,1348,1535,1534,1357$



I would be really happy if someone was able to answer any of these questions. :)





If I feel like being even crazier today, I might also consider doing Six 6s and Seven 7s as well.



CreditsCredits to ythomashu for finding these representations:

$$667=5.\overline5*5!+\sqrt{\frac{.\overline5}5}$$$$849=\left(\frac5{.\overline5}\right)^{\sqrt{\frac5{.\overline5}}}+5!$$$$887=\frac5{.5\%}-5!+5+\lim_{x\to.5}\frac x{x\cdot x}$$and fixing the typo for 1151:

$$1151=\frac{(5!-5)*5+.5}{.5}$$

Credits to sudzoof for finding a nice representation for 202:

$$202=\frac{5!+5-\frac{5!}5}{.5}$$

topics.title: Fair-and-square sets
topics.text:
A set of positive integers $S$ is called "fair-and-square" if for any $a,b\in S$, the digits of $a^2$ can be rearranged to form $b^2$.



One example of a fair-and-square set is $\{13,14\}$, because $13^2=169$ and $14^2=196$.



Another set is $\{42,69\}$ because $42^2=1764$ and $69^2=4761$.



Find all possible fair-and-square sets $S$ of positive integers, such that each element of $S$ is less than or equal to $1000$.

A list contains $20$ numbers.  For each positive integer $n$ from $1$ to $20$, the $n$th number in the list is either $\frac{1}{2}n$ or $2n$.  If the mean of the numbers in the list is exactly $12$, and the product of the numbers is $P$, what is the greatest possible value of $\frac{P}{20!}$?



Ans16




I'm wondering if there is a more elegant solution than mine.



My brute force solutionMy solution involved finding the sums of the $\frac{1}{2}n$'s ($105$) and the $2n$'s ($420$) and figuring out the minimum number of  $2n$'s to replace with $\frac{1}{2}n$'s to get a sum of 240.  Then I divided by $20!$, canceling out terms to get the answer.

topics.text:
This problem is an extension of the first one discussed in this video.



You start writing down the positive integers in order. Each one must be red, blue, or green. The rule is that you can not color three numbers, $a$, $b$, and $c$, such that $a + b = c$, all the same color. As an example, $3$, $5$, and $8$ can't all be the same color. What's the largest number that you can write down before you'd be forced to break the previously described rule?



I will share my conjectured answer.$23$
 This is how you get it.R,R,G,R,G,G,G,R,B,B,R,B,B,B,B,B,B,B,G,B,G,R,G
 If you get a greater number, let me know how you got it!



Here are two further extensions:



a) What if you're allowed to use four colors instead of just three? Five colors? (I have answers for these too, but I won't post them as I'm not super confident that they are correct.)



b) If we keep increasing the number of colors that can be used, does the number of numbers that can be written ever become infinite? Or, will you always be forced to stop at some point, no matter how many different colors you have?



Edit: I beat my own high score, still don't know if it's max possible.

topics.title: Chess & Math
topics.text:
So the other day, I was working through the possible positions in a chess game. I realized it was a lot more complicated than I thought it would be. So I thought it would be cool to run what I did past the AoPS community. So here's what I did:





[center]––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

The Possible Positions in a chess game

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––



So we start by taking the total number of squares on the board  $(64)$, and the number of pieces on the board $(32)$ and multiply them together to get the total number of positions in the game without complications: $64\times32=2,048.$ After this, we can take into account the places the pawns cannot go. Pawns cannot go into the back $8$ squares, and, for the sake of this computation, the top $8$ squares, because once they get there, they become a different piece. So, we have $16$ pawns, each of which have $16$ spaces they cannot go, so, from $2,048$, we subtract $16\times16=256$. We now have $1,792$ different possible positions. The next thing we should take into account is bishops, each bishop has $32$ spaces it cannot go, and there are $4$ bishops. So, from $1,792$, we subtract $4\times32=128$, which equals $1,664$ possible positions. The next thing is non-bishop pawn promotions. So we have $4$ pieces the pawn can become, and each of those pieces can go in $64$ spaces, so we add $4\times64=256$ to $1,664$, which equals $1,920$. The final thing we need to consider is bishop pawn promotions. This adds $32$ to our number, making the total number of possible positions in a chess game $$\boxed{1,952}$$––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––



So what I am looking for, is someone to point out anything I overlooked, or any mistakes I made. Thank you for your feedback!
